text: I think that most people assume that their boss has to manage them and they feel a little bit resentful that, why should I manage my boss? They're getting paid more. They are my manager. They have more responsibility.
speaker: Wes Kao
context: Lenny asks Wes why managing up is important and why people aren't doing it well. Wes explains that many people feel resistant to managing their boss because they think it's their manager's job to manage them, not the other way around. She argues that this mindset limits career growth and that those who embrace managing up will see significant benefits in their professional relationships and opportunities.
text_ko: 대부분 사람들은 상사가 자기를 관리해줘야 한다고 생각하는 것 같아요. 그래서 “내가 왜 상사를 관리해야 해?” 하고 좀 억울해하죠. 상사가 월급도 더 받고, 관리자니까 책임도 더 많으니까요.
text_zh: 我觉得大多数人都以为应该是老板管着他们，心里还有点抵触：干嘛我要管老板？人家拿得多，又是我的上司，责任也更重。
text_es: Creo que la mayoría de la gente asume que su jefe tiene que gestionarlos y siente cierto resentimiento: «¿por qué voy a gestionar a mi jefe? Les pagan más. Es mi jefe. Tiene más responsabilidad.»
key_sentence: most people assume that their boss has to manage them and they feel a little bit resentful
original_text: I think that most people assume that their boss has to manage them and they feel a little bit resentful that, why should I manage my boss? They're getting paid more. They are my manager. They have more responsibility. And you can continue to think that way and your career might be fine, but if you embrace that if you manage your boss, they're going to appreciate you much more, you're going to get more opportunities, you're going to have more trust with them, there's all these great things that happen when you decide to manage up.

vocabulary.definition: The state or fact of having a duty to deal with something or having control over someone.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a corporate environment, responsibility often refers to the obligations assigned to individuals or teams, impacting accountability and performance metrics.
vocabulary.nuance: While responsibility can denote a formal obligation, it also carries a connotation of ownership and accountability for outcomes.

vocabulary.definition: Feeling or expressing bitterness or indignation at having been treated unfairly.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the workplace, resentful attitudes can arise when employees feel undervalued or overburdened, potentially leading to decreased morale and productivity.
vocabulary.nuance: Resentment often implies a deeper emotional response that can affect workplace relationships and team dynamics.

vocabulary.definition: To take for granted or without proof; to accept something as true without verification.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, making assumptions can lead to misunderstandings and miscommunications, highlighting the importance of clarity and verification in decision-making.
vocabulary.nuance: While assuming can sometimes be necessary for efficiency, it often carries a risk of error, particularly in complex or high-stakes situations.

text: The idea behind what I call the state change method is that you should punctuate your monologues with state changes. So state changes are anything that shakes your audience awake and adds some variety.
speaker: Wes Kao
context: Lenny asks Wes about her concept of creating state change in presentations and meetings. Wes explains that most Zoom meetings involve one person talking while everyone else listens silently, which is draining for participants. The state change method involves breaking up monologues with interactive elements to keep the audience engaged and prevent them from zoning out during virtual presentations.
text_ko: 제가 '상태 전환 기법(state change method)'이라고 부르는 아이디어는, 긴 일방적 설명(혼자 하는 말)에 중간중간 '상태 전환(state changes)'을 집어넣으라는 거예요. 여기서 '상태 전환(state changes)'은 청중을 확 깨우고 분위기에 변화를 주는 모든 요소예요.
text_zh: 我说的“状态切换法”（state change method），就是说你在长篇发言里要穿插一些“状态变化”（state changes）。这些状态变化就是任何能把听众提神、抓回注意力、打破单调的东西。
text_es: La idea detrás de lo que llamo el método de cambio de estado (state change method) es que deberías intercalar en tus monólogos cambios de estado (state changes) que despierten a la audiencia. Esos cambios pueden ser cualquier cosa que sacuda al público y le aporte variedad.
key_sentence: Punctuate your monologues to shake your audience awake.
original_text: The idea behind what I call the state change method is that you should punctuate your monologues with state changes. So state changes are anything that shakes your audience awake and adds some variety. So it might be asking people to put something in the chat box. It might be switching from gallery view where you see everyone in that Brady Bunch grid and switch over to screen share, to share something and then switch back.

vocabulary.definition: To interrupt or enhance a flow of speech or writing with distinct elements, often to emphasize or clarify a point.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business presentations, punctuating a speech with visual aids or changes in tone can help maintain audience interest and highlight key messages.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'punctuate' can imply a positive enhancement, it may also suggest disruption if overused or poorly executed.

vocabulary.definition: The quality or state of being different or diverse; a range of different things.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing, offering a variety of products can attract a broader customer base and meet diverse consumer needs.
vocabulary.nuance: Variety often connotes a positive aspect of diversity, but too much variety can lead to confusion or decision fatigue among consumers.

vocabulary.definition: A group of individuals who are intended to receive a message or engage with a presentation, performance, or product.
vocabulary.businessContext: Understanding your target audience is crucial for effective marketing strategies and communication in business settings.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'audience' can imply passive reception, but in modern contexts, it often suggests active engagement and interaction.

text: So the idea behind what I call eyes lighting up is that when you're talking to someone and you're explaining something, you're teaching them, you're sharing your startup idea or whatever the normal response is people will want to be polite.
speaker: Wes Kao
context: Lenny asks about Wes's concept called 'eyes lighting up' in relation to state changes in meetings. Wes explains that when presenting or explaining ideas to people, most listeners will be polite and give generic positive responses. However, there are specific moments when someone becomes genuinely engaged - when their eyes literally light up with interest. This physical reaction provides valuable data about what content truly resonates with your audience.
text_ko: 제가 '눈빛이 반짝이는 순간(eyes lighting up)'이라고 부르는 개념의 핵심은, 누군가와 대화하면서 뭔가를 설명하거나 가르치거나 스타트업 아이디어를 공유할 때처럼 사람들은 보통 예의를 차리려 한다는 거예요.
text_zh: 我把这种现象叫“眼睛一亮”(eyes lighting up)：就是说，当你跟别人讲东西、解释某个概念、教人或者分享你的创业点子时，大家的正常反应通常只是出于礼貌客气一下。
text_es: La idea detrás de lo que yo llamo "ojos que se iluminan" es que cuando hablas con alguien y le explicas algo, le enseñas, le cuentas tu idea de empresa emergente (startup) o lo que sea, lo normal es que la gente quiera ser cortés.
key_sentence: Eyes light up when someone is genuinely interested.
original_text: So the idea behind what I call eyes lighting up is that when you're talking to someone and you're explaining something, you're teaching them, you're sharing your startup idea or whatever the normal response is people will want to be polite. So they'll nod and they'll say, 'Oh, okay, that's interesting.' But there's usually a moment in the conversation where their eyes light up because they are genuinely actually interested in what you are saying at that moment.

vocabulary.definition: The process of making something clear or understandable by providing details or context.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and business, explaining is essential for clarifying complex ideas, processes, or products to clients, investors, and team members.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'explaining' is straightforward, it implies a need for clarity and thoroughness, especially when dealing with intricate concepts or technical information.

vocabulary.definition: A reaction or reply to a question, request, or situation, often indicating understanding or engagement.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business interactions, a response can reflect customer feedback, stakeholder engagement, or team dynamics, and it is critical for assessing the effectiveness of communication strategies.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'response' can imply a level of engagement or feedback, and it is often used to gauge the success of presentations or discussions.

text: And ironically, the most senior people are best at managing up.
speaker: Wes Kao
context: Lenny asks why managing up is important and how to do it effectively. Wes addresses the misconception that senior people don't need to manage up anymore once they reach director or VP level. She explains that actually the opposite is true - the most successful senior leaders became successful precisely because they mastered the skill of managing up, understanding their bosses' concerns and proactively communicating to reduce their managers' workload.
text_ko: 아이러니하게도, 가장 선임된 분들이 상사 관리(managing up)를 가장 잘해요.
text_zh: 有意思的是，最资深的人反倒最会做向上管理 (managing up)。
text_es: Y, irónicamente, los más senior son los que mejor gestionan la relación con sus jefes (managing up).
key_sentence: the most senior people are best at managing up.
original_text: And ironically, the most senior people are best at managing up. This is why they got promoted in the first place because they were great at managing up to their bosses to understand what was worrying their bosses, what was keeping them up at night so that they could take that off their plate. They're great at keeping their bosses in the loop on what's happening so their bosses, aren't constantly having to ask and pepper them with questions every day.

vocabulary.definition: The practice of effectively communicating and working with one's superiors to ensure alignment and support for goals and initiatives.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, managing up is crucial for fostering positive relationships with senior management and ensuring that one's contributions are recognized and valued.
vocabulary.nuance: This term often implies a proactive approach to influence and support, rather than merely following directives.

vocabulary.definition: Individuals in an organization who hold high-level positions, typically with significant experience and authority.
vocabulary.businessContext: In corporate environments, senior people are often responsible for strategic decision-making and guiding the overall direction of the company.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply a level of respect and authority, but may also suggest a disconnect from day-to-day operations.

text: And so it went from being a conversation about yes or no, are you a helpful person or are you not, are you a team player or are you not into, hey, how do we make sure that the important right things get done?
speaker: Wes Kao
context: Lenny asks Wes for advice on how to say no effectively, mentioning his own struggles with declining requests politely. Wes shares a technique she learned from her colleague Alex, who would reframe 'no' conversations by discussing trade-offs instead of outright rejection. Rather than making it about whether someone is helpful or cooperative, Alex would explain what work would need to be deprioritized if he took on the new request, making it a strategic prioritization discussion.
text_ko: 결국 대화가 '도움이 되는 사람인가요, 아니면 아닌가요?', '팀 플레이어(team player)인가요, 아니면 아닌가요?' 같은 예·아니오형 논쟁에서 '어떻게 하면 중요한, 옳은 일들이 확실히 이뤄지게 할까요?'로 바뀌었어요.
text_zh: 所以讨论从那种“你是不是乐于助人、是不是团队合作者 (team player)”的“是或不是”变成了：嘿，我们怎么确保重要且正确的事能落到实处？
text_es: Y así pasó de ser una conversación de sí o no —¿eres alguien que ayuda o no? ¿trabajas en equipo o no?— a: oye, ¿cómo nos aseguramos de que se hagan las cosas que realmente importan?
key_sentence: how do we make sure that the important right things get done?
original_text: And so it went from being a conversation about yes or no, are you a helpful person or are you not, are you a team player or are you not into, hey, how do we make sure that the important right things get done? And so it's great for the person who you're saying no to and it's also great for Alex because whenever we had those conversations, I always thought that he was really thoughtful about making sure that the most important projects that we want to work on stayed prioritized.

vocabulary.definition: A team player is an individual who collaborates effectively with others to achieve common goals, demonstrating a cooperative attitude and a willingness to support teammates.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, being a team player is essential for fostering a collaborative work environment, particularly in projects that require cross-functional teamwork and communication.
vocabulary.nuance: While the term generally has a positive connotation, it can imply a lack of individual initiative if overemphasized in certain contexts.

vocabulary.definition: Important refers to something that holds significant value or priority, often requiring attention or action due to its impact or relevance.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, identifying important tasks or decisions is crucial for effective time management and strategic planning, ensuring that resources are allocated efficiently.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can be subjective, as what is considered important may vary based on individual perspectives or organizational goals.

vocabulary.definition: Get done refers to the act of completing a task or achieving a goal, often emphasizing efficiency and effectiveness in execution.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the fast-paced business environment, the ability to get things done is highly valued, as it reflects an individual's or team's productivity and commitment to meeting deadlines.
vocabulary.nuance: While it conveys a sense of urgency, it can sometimes imply a focus on speed over quality, so it should be used in contexts where both aspects are balanced.

text: A lot of times when we write a sentence, there's actually already a point of view or there's a point of view baked in, but you don't want it to be an accidental point of view.
speaker: Wes Kao
context: Lenny asks Wes for general writing advice beyond the concepts they've already discussed. Wes emphasizes the importance of studying the technical craft of writing rather than just mimicking social media content. She explains how writers often unconsciously embed a point of view in their sentences, and shares an example of giving feedback to a team member whose writing was inadvertently leading the reader toward a specific conclusion.
text_ko: 글을 쓸 때 문장에는 이미 어떤 관점이 배어 있는 경우가 많은데, 그 관점이 의도치 않게 들어가 있으면 안 돼요.
text_zh: 很多时候我们写一句话，话里就自带某种立场，但你不希望那是无意中夹带进去的。
text_es: Muchas veces, cuando escribimos una frase ya viene con un punto de vista implícito, pero no quieres que ese punto de vista sea accidental.
key_sentence: you don't want it to be an accidental point of view.
original_text: A lot of times when we write a sentence, there's actually already a point of view or there's a point of view baked in, but you don't want it to be an accidental point of view. I was just talking to my team member about this, she asked me to give her some feedback on something that she wrote and the way that she had written her paragraph was leading for the reader.

vocabulary.definition: A particular attitude or way of considering a matter; a perspective from which something is evaluated.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding different points of view can enhance decision-making and foster collaboration among diverse teams.
vocabulary.nuance: While it often refers to personal perspectives, in a business context, it can also imply the importance of aligning viewpoints for strategic objectives.

vocabulary.definition: Happening by chance or unexpectedly; not planned or intended.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business setting, accidental outcomes can lead to unintended consequences, highlighting the importance of strategic planning and risk management.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can carry a negative connotation when referring to mistakes or errors that could have been avoided with careful consideration.
